TRANSCRIPT OF PROCEEDINGS
THE HON CATHERINE HOLMES AC SC, Commissioner
THE ROYAL COMMISSION INTO THE ROBODEBT SCHEME
FRIDAY, 10 MARCH 2023 AT 10:01 AM (AEST)
DAY 46
MR JUSTIN GREGGERY KC, Senior Counsel Assisting
MR ANGUS SCOTT KC, Senior Counsel Assisting
MS SALWA MARSH, Counsel Assisting
MR DOUGLAS FREEBURN, Counsel Assisting
MS DOMINIQUE HOGAN-DORAN SC, for the Commonwealth
MS PHILIPPA KELLY, for the Commonwealth

COMMISSIONER: Yes, Mr Greggery.
MR GREGGERY: Yes. Before I hand to Ms Marsh, Commissioner, can I tender the exhibits on
the draft list numbered 8202A which commences on page 10, to the conclusion of the list
numbered 8391.
COMMISSIONER: Okay. Just bear with me for the moment. Sorry, 82 - - -
MR GREGGERY: 02A.
COMMISSIONER: Okay. Got it. Thank you. To the end of the list?
MR GREGGERY: To the end of list, yes. 8391.
COMMISSIONER: 8391. And does that include Professor Whiteford's report?
MS HOGAN-DORAN: Commissioner, that's just been brought to my attention. I had
understood that would be deferred at least until such time as the Commonwealth's letter
has been considered. Could I invite my friend to defer 8342 until after morning tea? 8391.
COMMISSIONER: After morning tea. I would like the report to be in evidence today, and if
the Commonwealth has issues about it, they can be raised. So are you happy to leave it until
after morning tea?
MR GREGGERY: I am, Commissioner, yes.
COMMISSIONER: Alright. So then the exhibits will go from 8202A to 8341 in accordance with
the list.
<EXHIBITS 8202A TO 8341 TENDERED AS PER THE EXHIBIT LIST
COMMISSIONER: I will just formally take the appearances, though, Mr Greggery. So are you
appearing with Ms Marsh?
MR GREGGERY: No, Ms Marsh has the first witness.
COMMISSIONER: Okay.
MR GREGGERY: I will hand over to her briefly. But there are five witnesses today, and after
the fifth, I will do a closing which will refer to some of the evidence and some of the issues.
COMMISSIONER: Alright. Thank you. And Ms Hogan-Doran?
MS HOGAN-DORAN: Commissioner, I appear with my learned friend Ms Kelly. And I've just
been instructed that the letter has gone to the Commission in respect of Professor

COMMISSIONER: Alright. Thank you. Yes, Ms Marsh.
MS MARSH: Thank you, Commissioner. I call Ms Taren Preston.
COMMISSIONER: Ms Preston, will you take an oath or affirmation?
MS PRESTON: Affirmation.
COMMISSIONER: Okay. Could you stand? Thank you.
<TAREN PRESTON, AFFIRMED
<EXAMINATION BY MS MARSH
COMMISSIONER: Yes, Ms Marsh.
MS MARSH: Thank you, Commissioner. Ms Preston, have you provided a Statement to the
Commission which you finalised on the 7th of March 2023?
MS PRESTON: Yes.
MS MARSH: Thank you. Is that true and correct to the best of your knowledge and belief?
MS PRESTON: Yes.
MS MARSH: Ms Preston, you worked as a social worker at Services Australia between 2005
and 2019. Is that right?
MS PRESTON: That's correct.
MS MARSH: And prior to that, you obtained a Bachelor of Social Work from Newcastle
University in 2014 - in 2004, rather?
MS PRESTON: That's correct, yes.
MS MARSH: Ms Preston, why did you study social work?
MS PRESTON: I think I was drawn to social work because I had a strong commitment to social
justice. Social work offers, as a career, the opportunity to work directly with people who
need support but also to work on a broader level, to advocate for fairness and social justice.
So I have absolutely loved my career as a social worker.
MS MARSH: And not long after you graduated from your bachelor's degree, in 2005 you
started working at Services Australia?

MS MARSH: Thank you. And you had a rapid trajectory. In 2007, you were promoted to the
role of a senior social worker?
MS PRESTON: Yes. Correct.
MS MARSH: And does that role involve additional responsibilities to the day-to-day casework
that you would otherwise do?
MS PRESTON: Yes, it did. Yes.
MS MARSH: Could you expand upon those?
MS PRESTON: Yes, I can. So I would maintain a level of casework, but I would also provide
support and development to a team of social workers. I would work in with the local
leadership teams. I would be there to support staff - service officers with any consults or
complex matters, deliver training and other duties as called.
MS MARSH: And for the duration of your time at Services Australia, you were working in that
more of a management role?
MS PRESTON: Correct. Yes. Yes.
MS MARSH: You mentioned in paragraph 27 of your Statement that you worked in the
Business Integrity Division and had built up a level of expertise in debt and fraud matters
from a social work perspective, including the psychosocial impacts of these matters - - -
MS PRESTON: Yes.
MS MARSH: - - - and the need for customers to be treated sensitively and with a high level of
customer service skills.
MS PRESTON: Correct. Yes.
MS MARSH: Could you expand upon the best practices - - -
MS PRESTON: Yes.
MS MARSH: - - - when dealing with people in that space?
MS PRESTON: So I was involved in setting up the first social work team that was in Business
Integrity. What - what I was able to - what the team was able to achieve was being able to
support the customers who were presenting with debt issues, to handle them with care and
sensitivity. Also, to make sure that the Department understood any other vulnerabilities or
concerns that were impacting the customer that might either have attributed to the reason
why they had an overpayment or might provide direction on how to manage the debt

moving forward, including if there was a need to consider waiving the recovery of debt under
those special circumstances.
MS MARSH: So would I be right in saying that in addition to both management
responsibilities, you bring to your evidence today specific experience in fraud and debt
matters?
MS PRESTON: I believe so, yes.
MS MARSH: Thank you.
COMMISSIONER: When was that, the setting up the first Business Integrity social work team,
roughly? I don't need precise dates.
MS PRESTON: From 2009 - and I worked until 2010 in that role. I moved out of that team to
another opportunity, but I believe that service did continue for a little bit of time but then
was - might have been rolled into general servicing afterwards.
COMMISSIONER: Okay. Thank you.
MS MARSH: Ms Preston, I would now like to move to the part of your Statement where you
give evidence on your role as a social worker at Centrelink before the introduction of the
Robodebt Scheme, and that evidence is set out in paragraphs 13 to 21 of your Statement.
MS PRESTON: Yes.
MS MARSH: Can you assist the Commission in explaining the work that you did as a social
worker prior to Robodebt?
MS PRESTON: Yes. So the usual work of a social worker when I first started in the
Department was working with individuals as they came through the service centre. So it was
a really diverse range of people who were referred to social work, but it tended to be the
customer or the clients who were at most risk. So it would frequently be supporting people
with - in regards to crisis intervention, assessment, social casework consultation about
matters that were a little bit more complex. So it could be anything - or anyone from a mum
in the office with her little children fleeing domestic violence to somebody presenting in an
acute mental health state who needed some support, someone recently unemployed who
was navigating a major personal crisis. So my job was to support them, to understand their
circumstances, to provide some direct servicing, so counselling, crisis intervention, follow-up
support as well, safeguarding if there were some worries and concerns about their health
and wellbeing. The other part of my role would then be following up around Centrelink
matters to make sure that they were receiving the right entitlements, that they were - any
plans that the Department had in place were fair and reasonable and took account of
their - their unique circumstances.
MS MARSH: So would it be right to summarise that by saying that you had a role that was

ensuring that those customers were able to access their entitlements within the Centrelink
system?
MS PRESTON: Correct. And that if there were parts of the legislation or the guide on how
to - how to support them, that they were able to access those pathways. What I found in my
career was that the more complex the customer's circumstances, there was more - the more
complex the Centrelink matter. So a part of the social work role was navigating that and
making sure that they weren't falling through the gaps, and they weren't missing out or
being treated unfairly.
MS MARSH: And can you tell me on a day-to-day basis how many - how many customers you
would see?
MS PRESTON: Yes. Before - it was busy, but it was manageable. So my - my recollection was
we would have an appointment schedule, maybe three appointments. That would also give
me time throughout the day to respond to any - what they would refer to as walk-in crisis
presentations. So maybe - it felt manageable at that point. So, you know, appointments - I
knew what was coming in my week. And I was able to also have that time to follow up on any
reports or assessments I was doing and the ongoing follow-up work with clients who were at
the highest risk.
MS MARSH: So to summarise, it would be right to say you would have about five - - -
MS PRESTON: Yes.
MS MARSH: Around about five - - -
MS PRESTON: Yes, yes.
MS MARSH: - - - people come into your office every day and have that opportunity to speak
with them?
MS PRESTON: Yes.
MS MARSH: And then do your desk work?
MS PRESTON: Yes.
MS MARSH: And this was all before the inception of the Scheme?
MS PRESTON: Yes.
MS MARSH: Okay.
COMMISSIONER: Ms Preston, you are talking quite fast.

COMMISSIONER: Just relax.
MS PRESTON: It's a bit hard – easier said than done.
COMMISSIONER: Have a drink of water and be as calm as you possibly can.
MS PRESTON: Okay. Thank you.
MS MARSH: And before the inception of the Robodebt Scheme, when someone would come
to your desk, what sort of inquiries would you make with them?
MS PRESTON: Would I make with them?
MS MARSH: Yes. What would you ask them?
MS PRESTON: Yes, I would start by trying to build some rapport to understand what was
happening for them that day, to get a sense of - so I guess it depended on what the
presentation was. So I would need to apply different, I guess, approaches depending on if it
was a young person who was experiencing homelessness, compared to somebody fleeing
domestic violence. I would need to shift my focus depending on their presentation.
MS MARSH: Okay.
MS PRESTON: Yes.
COMMISSIONER: Look, can I just add, the reason I want you to talk slower is because I'm
deeply interested in what you are saying, and I want to hear and understand it all. So thank
you.
MS PRESTON: Thank you.
MS MARSH: And what sort of questions would you ask people who came in who were
dealing with debt issues?
MS PRESTON: Before or after Robodebt?
MS MARSH: Before Robodebt.
MS PRESTON: Before Robodebt. I would usually have a good referral, would be something
that was - that I would know beforehand. So I would have a good handover, that I would
have already had an understanding on the matter at hand and where things were up to.
MS MARSH: Is that because someone will have referred them to you?
MS PRESTON: Yes.

MS MARSH: And so you will be able to access their file?
MS PRESTON: Yes. And they would - and I would have, like, a verbal handover as well. So
there would be a consultation before I would make contact or go and see the customer. So I
would have a good strong understanding on where we are up to. And then when I spoke
with the person, I would get a sense on where they were at. So I would try to build that
rapport so that they could let me, I guess, assist them through it. I would be really - I was
always very curious and conscious of the way that debts interacted with people who were on
income support already in that we were - I guess we were - people were already perhaps
experiencing social exclusion because of the income support. So it - debts hit people in those
circumstances differently. So I would be trying to get an understanding on how the debt was
impacting them and what it meant for their health and wellbeing, what it meant for their
family. And, you know, at times, what it meant for their safety, if it was too overwhelming.
MS MARSH: And so am I right in saying that you would consult the file and look at the
referral notes - - -
MS PRESTON: Yes.
MS MARSH: - - - and then speak to those customers and then identify which support
work - - -
MS PRESTON: Yes. Yes.
MS MARSH: - - - channels to present to them and also what you needed to do within the
Centrelink system?
MS PRESTON: Yes. Yes. And can I add to that - - -
MS MARSH: Yes.
MS PRESTON: - - - probably just a bit, that in the - before Robodebt, I would often be sought
out to give a professional assessment in the referrals. So perhaps a service officer or a team
leader would say, "Look, we are curious about if there are special circumstances and we are
seeking out your opinion and professional assessment on that.” So outside of that - working
with the customer, I would then have another role in preparing a report to recommend
perhaps special circumstances were applied or considered so that the recovery of the debt
was managed in respect of their particular circumstances.
MS MARSH: And were the people who were reaching out to you Compliance Officers and
AROs?
MS PRESTON: Yes.
MS MARSH: And in addition to working with recipients, is it right to say that you also
sometimes worked with staff from Centrelink?

MS PRESTON: Yes.
MS MARSH: And what sort of issues would staff from Centrelink come to you about?
MS PRESTON: Yes. So before - it was maybe a personal issue that they were navigating. We
would also be available to provide a debrief if there had been a situation in the office, so, you
know, customer aggression or a critical event or something, you know, that was a bit
sensitive. Also, we would support teams with issues of team dynamics and help them work
out ways forward through those.
MS MARSH: Roughly how many times a week would you say you saw staff members before
the inception of - - -
MS PRESTON: Before, maybe once a week or it was - the other thing about it, it was more
planned. So we would - they would book in a time for social workers to come - - -
MS MARSH: Okay.
MS PRESTON: - - - so it wasn't as reactive.
MS MARSH: Okay. I wanted now to move to the shift that you observed at the time that the
Robodebt Scheme was implemented, and the evidence that you give in respect of that starts
at paragraph 22 of your statement. And you say that you noticed an immediate increase in
your workload. Can you expand upon what you first noticed?
MS PRESTON: Yes. So I think because I was also coming back from maternity leave, I had
missed, I guess, some rollout and build-up. So when I came back, the change was very stark
to the DHS that I had left before mat leave. What I noticed was that there was an increase in
customers being referred to me. There was an increase in the level of distress that they were
experiencing and an increase in people being in that state due to the Robodebts and the
debt notice.
MS MARSH: Can I - can I take you through each of those.
MS PRESTON: Yes.
MS MARSH: So when you say that there was an increase in the number of referrals you had,
you give evidence in your Statement of seeing up to sort of 10 customers a day.
MS PRESTON: Yes. Correct. Yes.
MS MARSH: So that's - you have doubled the number of customers you're seeing.
MS PRESTON: Doubled the number, yes.
MS MARSH: And did you - did you have to increase your work hours in order to do that?

MS PRESTON: I did. I - yes, I did increase my work hours. It was really - it was hard - I guess it
was a hard balance because it was very hard to know that there were so many people who
were requiring social work support. So we - you know, we wanted to make sure that we
were talking and supporting as many people as we could.
MS MARSH: And did that also have a knock-on impact on your other responsibilities, your
desk work, your management responsibilities?
MS PRESTON: Yes. It did. Yes. So we were all kind of hitting the ground and trying to
get - connect with as many people as we could. As a manager, some days that was the best
way I could support my team, by pitching in and supporting them through the caseload as
well.
MS MARSH: Were any additional social workers taken on to meet the increase in demand?
MS PRESTON: No, there wasn't. My recollection would be that in that period, we
weren't - there were no additional social work resources. But also at the same time, we were
losing really good social workers from the Department.
MS MARSH: And was your impression that Centrelink was meeting the demand for social
workers?
MS PRESTON: No. No. Not at all.
MS MARSH: You identified a series of things before that you noticed had changed, and
another one was the nature of customer distress.
MS PRESTON: Yes. Yes.
MS MARSH: Could I ask you to expand upon that?
MS PRESTON: Because I had had experience working with the debt matters in the past, this
also stood out to me. What I noticed was that the people who were referred to me were - I
guess it was - was moving much more quickly than it usually would, and they weren't being
given, I guess, a right of reply. Often they weren't really understanding how the debt had
come about. And because it was often some years beforehand, it was difficult to access what
they were being asked. So what I noticed was when people came through the doors, they
had already spoken to people on the phone, Compliance Officers. Perhaps they had also
already been contacted by some external debt recovery agencies. So they were very
heightened, very distressed.
MS MARSH: Okay. And I wondered if I could call out paragraph 29 of your Statement. You
say:
I was acutely concerned with identifying risk of suicide.

MS MARSH: Can you expand upon that concern?
MS PRESTON: Yes. Which - sorry, which - - -
MS MARSH: 29. It will be on the screen - - -
MS PRESTON: Yes. Okay.
MS MARSH: - - - but it is also on your desk as well - - -
MS PRESTON: Yes.
MS MARSH: - - - whichever is easier for you to review.
MS PRESTON: Yes. So with - in that period of Robodebt, my attention turned much more
keenly to checking in on people's mental health. Often people would say - make a statement
like, "Well, I'm just going to put myself in front of a truck," or, "I'm going to throw myself off
a bridge.” Or they would make - their presentation - they would be low effect, a sense of
hopelessness. So it became fairly standard that when someone was coming in for a debt that
I would, I guess, move forward into what might be called a suicide risk assessment. So
sometimes people would say, "Look, no, it's not that bad, but thank you for asking.” And we
would go down a pathway of making sure that they had enough support in place, because it
still, you know, was an acutely distressing time.
Other times, people would let me know that they were having thoughts of suicide. In that - in
those times, which was very frequent in Robodebt, I would try and do some safeguarding
with them to get a sense of if they had a plan - if they had a plan, if they had means to enact
that plan. Who was at home with them at the time? If they were connected to a GP, if they
were connected to a community mental health service. I would then - based on what we
discussed and what we had identified as worries, I might - sorry, I - if I was worried, I would
make a referral out to the mental health team, the acute crisis team, depending on what
state it was in. Sometimes people were happy for me to do that and wanted to access
support. At times, I needed to release information in the public interest due to the duty of
care I had. Then I would liaise with the mental health service, hand over to them and they
would respond as they - they saw fit. So sometimes that would be a connection with the
community mental health team. An acute mental health service would go and see the person
to provide that support.
MS MARSH: Ms Preston, I wanted to take you to something else you say in your Statement in
paragraph 32.
MS PRESTON: Yes.
MS MARSH: You said:

I also observed the customers I spoke with under the Robodebt Scheme become increasingly
hopeless. They felt hopeless because there was no way out.
Could you expand upon the impression you received as to why they felt there was no way
out?
MS PRESTON: Yes. My impression was that there was a level of unfairness that they were
being presented with. So there was - there wasn't a way to navigate through it. And
Centrelink - DHS - it's an exceptionally big system. And when you're fighting a big system and
you're already vulnerable, it can feel very overwhelming.
MS MARSH: Would it be right to say people were getting lost in the system?
MS PRESTON: People were lost in the system. They weren't - it was really tricky to identify a
way forward, particularly where they couldn't produce documents they were asked for. Not
because they didn't want to, it's because perhaps, you know, they had other vulnerabilities
perhaps and it was difficult to navigate. And then you were needing to go back to old
employers. And there was such a short period of time requested to be able to get them. But
on the other hand, Centrelink wasn't being forthcoming on how the debts were raised in the
first place. So it felt - they saw that sense of unfairness. And for me, what I observed is that it
looked like it felt crushing.
MS MARSH: You gave evidence earlier that one of the things you would often do is - or prior
to the Robodebt Scheme is liaise with AROs and Compliance Officers and, in a sense, provide
them with information and your professional opinions and that that would shape the way
that their issues were managed. Did you feel that you were still able to do that during the
course of the Robodebt Scheme?
MS PRESTON: I still did it. So I would still do what I had always done and what I had built
expertise in. What I noticed afterwards is that, first of all, my - my assessments weren't
sought out. And then if I went and advocated for a certain part of the legislation to be
enacted - so special circumstances - that might be anything from, "Just pause - can we
just" - you know, "Can we just pause this matter for a second while we understand what's
going on," to perhaps saying, you know, "Let's - yes, there's an overpayment, but in the
public interest, there's special circumstances. We could waive the recovery.” So my approach
didn't necessarily change. I was still doing what I would have considered pretty thorough
professional assessments. I was often being able to gather third-party evidence from other
independent sources to support my recommendation.
After Robodebt, I felt that my professional assessments and recommendations were perhaps
looked down upon. Some - there was a mantra that would come back to me, which has stuck
with me. "So sad, too bad," was sometimes what I had heard people say when I indicated
that somebody was in a great deal of distress over the matter. But also the advice just wasn't
seen as valuable, which was a big shift. So it - sometimes it felt it was met with a bit of - a bit
of scorn, that there was a - there seemed to be a view that social workers didn't have a place
in that advocacy and professional assessment part of the debt matter.

MS MARSH: Would I be right to say there was an attitudinal shift - - -
MS PRESTON: Yes, there was.
MS MARSH: - - - that accompanied the process?
MS PRESTON: Yes, there was a culture shift. Yes.
MS MARSH: Can I take you now to the part of the Statement where you talk about your work
with Centrelink staff, which starts at paragraph 39.
MS PRESTON: Yes.
MS MARSH: In that paragraph, you say you began to start your days earlier, at around 8 am:
...so that I could be available to staff.
MS PRESTON: Yes.
MS MARSH: So does that reflect that in addition to doubling customers, you were now
seeing staff much more frequently?
MS PRESTON: I was, yes. So I think the office doors were opening at 8:30. So I would make a
point of getting to the office before 8 o'clock so that I could be available to have my door
open.
MS MARSH: Was that because staff members needed to prepare for the day?
MS PRESTON: They needed to prepare for the day. Staff were under increasing - just they
were under an increased pressure as well, and they were really good staff who wanted to
help and were also, I guess, in their own space trying to fight against the system and raising
their concerns. But some - you know, some days there would be two staff in the office in
tears, high levels of anxiety, that I provided debrief and support to to get them ready for the
doors to open.
MS MARSH: And that's before your day - - -
MS PRESTON: That's before the day started, yes.
MS MARSH: If I could call out paragraph 41. You give some evidence consistent with that,
saying that:
Each morning, staff were anxious about their day ahead.
MS PRESTON: Yes.

During Robodebt … people were increasingly saying they felt ashamed and wanted to quit.
MS PRESTON: Yes.
MS MARSH: Can you expand upon that impression that you received?
MS PRESTON: Yes. So, you know, my experience up to that point is that Centrelink staff were
by and large really proud of the work they did. They really got a lot of professional and
personal identity and satisfaction on helping those most at risk. During Robodebt, they
were - that wasn't the case. They were feeling very - they were feeling ashamed. They were
feeling anxious. It was really difficult for them not to be able to support the customer in front
of them in the way that they felt would be fair.
MS MARSH: Ms Preston, in the next paragraph at 42 you give evidence of a particularly bad
day that you can recall.
MS PRESTON: Yes.
MS MARSH: Could you share your experience of that day?
MS PRESTON: Yes. So this was a particularly bad day, but elements of this featured every
day. But that day, I debriefed two staff members who were in tears. And then as the day
proceeded, there were 10 referrals for customers at risk of suicide or who were in high levels
of distress due to debts.
MS MARSH: Ms Preston, you have given evidence about working with customers and
staff - - -
MS PRESTON: Yes.
MS MARSH: - - - who were in situations of distress.
MS PRESTON: Mmm.
MS MARSH: Would be prepared to share your experience of the impact that that had on
you?
MS PRESTON: Yes. Yes, I can. I have a really clear memory of being outside the office, so
parking my car, getting ready to go to work and having this impending sense of doom. I later
identified that that was anxiety that I was feeling myself. It was really tricky because I had
two little kids at the time, so I needed to balance my own wellbeing. There was a lot of
demands placed on social workers. I could see that there was frustrations because we
couldn't be available for everybody, but my impressions were we were trying our hardest. I
ended up talking to my doctor about it. My doctor cautioned me that I was probably heading
towards a psychological injury myself, that she was seeing signs of an adjustment disorder,

MS MARSH: Thank you. I wanted to now move to the next part your Statement where you
talk about the feedback that you were receiving from staff and the feedback that you were
providing to management.
MS PRESTON: Yes.
MS MARSH: And so I wanted to ask you, were you raising concerns about what you were
seeing in - amongst customers and staff, you escalating those concerns?
MS PRESTON: Yes, I was. So from the first training package where the income averaging was
talked about, even as a social worker I could see that it - it didn't make a lot of sense to me.
And because I had had the opportunity to work alongside compliance staff in my previous
roles, I knew how much care and manual calculations were going on to get the debt right.
And they were really committed to making sure every dollar and every cent was correct. So I
knew from the outset that the Scheme didn't seem to make a lot of even just mathematical
sense. So that was raised. Again, we were told that it - you know, this was a transformation,
and it was, you know, the way of the future, and it was - we were moving ahead with it. But I
could see it didn't pass that pub test. It just didn't seem fair, particularly around raising a
debt and then asking for evidence. Those kind of elements of it just wasn't the way that the
Public Service was making decisions in the past. It was a big shift.
MS MARSH: And am I right in saying that to the extent that you raised those concerns, there
wasn't any meaningful engagement with them?
MS PRESTON: No, I think - so I - I was raising concerns and so were my colleagues in social
work and service officers. There was probably two ways that that feedback went. So
sometimes it was ignored. And, you know, we - social workers have no part in policy and
procedure. So, you know, leave that to the experts. The other way it would be met with was
maybe some acknowledgment that, yes, there are some problems, but no pathway to
advocate through it. Like I said earlier, a key part of social work is advocating for fairness. So
it was difficult to not see that - a pathway to be able to raise concerns.
And I was particularly mindful to make sure I was giving really concrete examples and
kind - trying to articulate there were unintended policy consequences that were impacting
really vulnerable people. But I didn't feel that it could get the traction. I raised the
feedback - whenever I had the opportunity at this point, particularly when I was observing
that increase in distress, I - any time there was a manager higher than myself - so EL2, SES,
you know, upwards - we would be given an opportunity to meet with them and this feedback
was given, but it didn't go anywhere. We were - it was really hard to tell these stories and to
advocate for our clients but be hit with a - you know, be hit - to be stonewalled about it.
MS MARSH: Ms Preston, I wanted to ask you one final question, which is to ask you to
expand upon something you say in paragraph 51.
MS PRESTON: Yes.

MS MARSH: You say:
The best way I can think of to describe my experience was that I felt like I suffered a moral
injury - doing myself damage by continuing to work within an unfair system of oppression
that I thought was designed to get people rather than to support them...
Could you expand upon that experience?
